sets.title: Anthem for Doomed Youth
sets.author: Wilfred Owen
sets.source: Anthem for Doomed Youth, in Poems (ed. Siegfried Sassoon), Chatto & Windus, 1920 (written 1917)
sets.headnote: Wilfred Owen, a British officer on the Western Front, drafted this sonnet in 1917 at Craiglockhart War Hospital, where he was being treated for shell shock. He was killed in November 1918 and the poem was published after his death.
sets.body:
What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?
— Only the monstrous anger of the guns.
Only the stuttering rifles' rapid rattle
Can patter out their hasty orisons.
No mockeries now for them; no prayers nor bells;
Nor any voice of mourning save the choirs,—
The shrill, demented choirs of wailing shells;
And bugles calling for them from sad shires.

What candles may be held to speed them all?
Not in the hands of boys, but in their eyes
Shall shine the holy glimmers of goodbyes.
The pallor of girls' brows shall be their pall;
Their flowers the tenderness of patient minds,
And each slow dusk a drawing-down of blinds.

pair.title: The Man He Killed
pair.author: Thomas Hardy
pair.source: The Man He Killed, in Time's Laughingstocks and Other Verses, Macmillan, 1909 (first published 1902)
pair.headnote: Thomas Hardy wrote this dramatic monologue during the Boer War (1899–1902). The speaker is an ordinary working man; a nipperkin is a small measure of drink, and to 'list is to enlist.
pair.body:
“Had he and I but met
By some old ancient inn,
We should have sat us down to wet
Right many a nipperkin!

“But ranged as infantry,
And staring face to face,
I shot at him as he at me,
And killed him in his place.

“I shot him dead because —
Because he was my foe,
Just so: my foe of course he was;
That's clear enough; although

“He thought he'd 'list, perhaps,
Off-hand like — just as I —
Was out of work — had sold his traps —
No other reason why.

“Yes; quaint and curious war is!
You shoot a fellow down
You'd treat if met where any bar is,
Or help to half-a-crown.”

questions.model:
Owen's sonnet systematically measures the rituals of a Christian funeral against the battlefield and finds that the soldiers receive none of them. The opening rhetorical question, "What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?", sets up the contrast: bells honour the individual dead, but the simile reduces the soldiers to animals slaughtered in mass. The answer substitutes noise for ritual: "Only the monstrous anger of the guns." The alliteration and onomatopoeia of "the stuttering rifles' rapid rattle" mimic gunfire, while "patter out their hasty orisons" turns prayer into something mechanical and rushed. Even the choir becomes "The shrill, demented choirs of wailing shells", personification that makes the artillery a mad parody of mourning, and the speaker dismisses conventional religion as "mockeries".

The sestet answers the second question by relocating the rituals to those left at home. Candles become "the holy glimmers of goodbyes" in boys' eyes, the funeral cloth becomes "The pallor of girls' brows", and the final image, "each slow dusk a drawing-down of blinds", turns a household custom of mourning into a daily, unending grief. The sonnet's movement from the clamour of the octave to this hushed, slow close enacts Owen's point: the only true funeral rites are the private sorrow of those who loved the dead.

questions.model:
Both poems challenge comfortable public attitudes to war, but from opposite directions. Owen, writing as an officer grieving his men, attacks the belief that soldiers die nobly and are honoured; Hardy, voicing an ordinary infantryman, attacks the belief that the man one kills is truly an enemy. Owen's challenge is elegiac and angry; Hardy's is quiet, ironic and all the more unsettling for its plainness.

The poems differ first in how they see the soldier. Owen's soldiers are an anonymous mass, "these who die as cattle", denied even individual burial rites, and his outrage lies in that dehumanisation. Hardy works in reverse: he restores individuality to the enemy. The man killed becomes a mirror of the speaker, one who "thought he'd 'list, perhaps, / Off-hand like — just as I — / Was out of work". The dashes imitate a mind slowly discovering that the "foe" was simply another poor man, so the accepted category of enemy collapses.

Voice and form intensify each challenge. Owen adopts the elevated sonnet, the form of love and praise, and fills it with "monstrous anger" and "wailing shells", so the form itself becomes ironic: this is an anthem that refuses to celebrate. Hardy's short ballad-like quatrains and colloquial diction, "Right many a nipperkin!", give us a pub conversation rather than a lament. The jaunty rhythm clashes with the subject, and the hesitation of "because — / Because he was my foe" exposes the official justification as hollow.

The endings show the difference most clearly. Owen closes in mourning, "each slow dusk a drawing-down of blinds", moving the reader to grief for those at home. Hardy closes with understatement: "Yes; quaint and curious war is!" The inadequate adjectives are deliberately absurd, inviting the reader to supply the moral judgement the speaker cannot. Owen therefore makes us feel the cost of war, while Hardy makes us question its logic, and together they dismantle both the glory of dying and the justice of killing.

sets.title: Crossing the Bar
sets.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
sets.source: Crossing the Bar, in Demeter and Other Poems, Macmillan, 1889
sets.headnote: Alfred, Lord Tennyson, Poet Laureate of Britain, wrote this short lyric in 1889, aged eighty, and asked that it be placed at the end of all collections of his poems. The 'bar' is a sandbank across a harbour mouth.
sets.body:
Sunset and evening star,
And one clear call for me!
And may there be no moaning of the bar,
When I put out to sea,

But such a tide as moving seems asleep,
Too full for sound and foam,
When that which drew from out the boundless deep
Turns again home.

Twilight and evening bell,
And after that the dark!
And may there be no sadness of farewell,
When I embark;

For tho' from out our bourne of Time and Place
The flood may bear me far,
I hope to see my Pilot face to face
When I have crost the bar.

pair.title: Up-Hill
pair.author: Christina Rossetti
pair.source: Up-Hill, in Goblin Market and Other Poems, Macmillan, 1862
pair.headnote: Christina Rossetti was an English poet of strong religious faith. This poem, first published in 1861, is a dialogue between a traveller and an unnamed guide.
pair.body:
Does the road wind up-hill all the way?
Yes, to the very end.
Will the day's journey take the whole long day?
From morn to night, my friend.

But is there for the night a resting-place?
A roof for when the slow dark hours begin.
May not the darkness hide it from my face?
You cannot miss that inn.

Shall I meet other wayfarers at night?
Those who have gone before.
Then must I knock, or call when just in sight?
They will not keep you standing at that door.

Shall I find comfort, travel-sore and weak?
Of labour you shall find the sum.
Will there be beds for me and all who seek?
Yea, beds for all who come.

questions.model: Tennyson represents death as a calm sea voyage, so that dying becomes a departure rather than an ending. The "clear call" at sunset summons the speaker, and dying is simply the moment "When I put out to sea." He prays for "no moaning of the bar", the sound of waves breaking over the sandbank, which doubles as the moaning of mourners: he hopes for a crossing without turbulence or grief. Instead he wants a tide "Too full for sound and foam", an image of quiet completeness, and the soul that "drew from out the boundless deep / Turns again home", suggesting death is a return to where life began. The voyage ends with the "Pilot", a metaphor for God, whom he hopes to see "face to face", turning the metaphor into an expression of faith.

questions.model:
Both poets imagine death as the end of a journey that leads to rest with God, but they differ in where they place the emphasis. Tennyson's speaker looks forward with serene, almost eager acceptance to the voyage itself; Rossetti's traveller looks back on the effort of life and needs reassurance that rest will come.

The journeys themselves reveal this difference. In Text 1 the journey is a sea crossing begun at sunset, and the speaker asks only that it be gentle: "may there be no moaning of the bar, / When I put out to sea". Death is the short passage over a sandbank. In Text 2 the journey is life itself, a road that winds "up-hill all the way", lasting "From morn to night". Rossetti emphasises the length and labour of living, and death is the "resting-place" reached at nightfall.

Voice reinforces these attitudes. Tennyson's single speaker uses exclamations and prayerful wishes, "And may there be no sadness of farewell", so his tone is composed and hopeful. Rossetti divides the voice into an anxious questioner, "Shall I find comfort, travel-sore and weak?", and a calm guide, dramatising doubt that must be answered.

Both poems end in faith. Tennyson hopes "to see my Pilot face to face", a personal meeting with God, while Rossetti's guide promises community and shelter: "Those who have gone before" and "beds for all who come". Tennyson's comfort is individual and visionary; Rossetti's is collective and domestic, but both turn death from a fear into a homecoming.

sets.title: The Tyger
sets.author: William Blake
sets.source: The Tyger, in Songs of Innocence and of Experience, 1794
sets.headnote: William Blake was an English poet, painter and engraver who printed and hand-coloured his own books. This poem appears in Songs of Experience, a companion to his earlier Songs of Innocence, which contains a poem called 'The Lamb'.
sets.body:
Tyger Tyger, burning bright,
In the forests of the night;
What immortal hand or eye,
Could frame thy fearful symmetry?

In what distant deeps or skies,
Burnt the fire of thine eyes?
On what wings dare he aspire?
What the hand, dare seize the fire?

And what shoulder, & what art,
Could twist the sinews of thy heart?
And when thy heart began to beat,
What dread hand? & what dread feet?

What the hammer? what the chain,
In what furnace was thy brain?
What the anvil? what dread grasp,
Dare its deadly terrors clasp!

When the stars threw down their spears
And water'd heaven with their tears:
Did he smile his work to see?
Did he who made the Lamb make thee?

Tyger Tyger burning bright,
In the forests of the night:
What immortal hand or eye,
Dare frame thy fearful symmetry?

questions.model: Blake represents the tiger as a living flame, a creature of terrible beauty. The opening apostrophe, "Tyger Tyger, burning bright", makes its striped coat glow like fire, and the contrast with "the forests of the night" makes that brightness more vivid and more threatening, as though the tiger were the only light in a dark and dangerous world. Fire also suggests energy and destruction: in the second stanza the speaker wonders where "Burnt the fire of thine eyes", so the tiger's gaze itself is fierce. Finally, the question "What the hand, dare seize the fire?" suggests that making the tiger required a daring, even dangerous creator, so the imagery of fire shapes both the beast and the mysterious power behind it.

questions.model:
Blake explores the tiger's creation through a relentless sequence of questions that are never answered, and through the extended metaphor of a blacksmith's forge. The effect is to present creation as violent, physical labour by a power the speaker can neither see nor comprehend.

The forge metaphor dominates the fourth stanza: "What the hammer? what the chain, / In what furnace was thy brain? / What the anvil? what dread grasp". The creator becomes a smith hammering the tiger into shape, and the tiger's brain is something heated and beaten like metal. The short, heavily stressed trochaic lines and repeated "what" fall like hammer blows, while the plosive sounds of "dread" and "deadly" make the work menacing. Even the body is forged: the creator must "twist the sinews of thy heart", a verb that suggests strain and force.

The questions accumulate until the most disturbing one: "Did he who made the Lamb make thee?" The gentle lamb and the fierce tiger may share one maker, which forces the reader to consider how a good creator could make something so terrible. The final stanza repeats the first but changes "Could" to "Dare", so the closing question moves from capability to audacity. The poem ends without answers, leaving the creator's nature a mystery.

questions.model:
The claim is largely persuasive. Blake gives the tiger an intense physical presence, but every image of the animal turns into a question about its maker, and the poem's real subject is the unsettling possibility that a single creator is responsible for both innocence and ferocity.

The tiger is certainly vivid. It is "burning bright", with fiery eyes, a heart of twisted "sinews" and a brain formed in a "furnace". Yet Blake never describes the tiger hunting or moving; he describes it being made. The repeated question, "What immortal hand or eye, / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?", shifts attention from the creature to the "immortal hand" behind it. "Fearful symmetry" is the poem's central paradox: the tiger's perfect design inspires both awe and terror, so beauty and danger are inseparable.

The climax confirms that the poem concerns good and evil. "Did he who made the Lamb make thee?" recalls the lamb of Songs of Innocence, a traditional symbol of Christ and gentleness. If one God made both, then the violence and danger of experience are part of the divine plan, and the speaker cannot tell whether that God "smile[d] his work to see". The preceding image, "When the stars threw down their spears / And water'd heaven with their tears", has the cosmic resonance of a fall or rebellion, widening the poem from zoology to theology.

Structure deepens the mystery. The final stanza repeats the first almost exactly, creating a circle with no answer, but one word changes: "Could frame" becomes "Dare frame". The question is no longer whether such a creation was possible but how anyone dared it, which emphasises moral rather than physical power.

It would be too strong to say the animal does not matter: without its concrete, dazzling energy, the questions would be abstract. But the tiger functions as a symbol through which Blake confronts the coexistence of beauty, terror and goodness in creation, so the claim is convincing.

sets.title: I wandered lonely as a cloud
sets.author: William Wordsworth
sets.source: I wandered lonely as a cloud, in Poems, Longman, 1815 (first version published 1807)
sets.headnote: William Wordsworth was an English Romantic poet who lived in the Lake District. The poem draws on a walk he took with his sister Dorothy beside Ullswater in April 1802; this is his revised version of 1815.
sets.body:
I wandered lonely as a cloud
That floats on high o'er vales and hills,
When all at once I saw a crowd,
A host, of golden daffodils;
Beside the lake, beneath the trees,
Fluttering and dancing in the breeze.

Continuous as the stars that shine
And twinkle on the milky way,
They stretched in never-ending line
Along the margin of a bay:
Ten thousand saw I at a glance,
Tossing their heads in sprightly dance.

The waves beside them danced; but they
Out-did the sparkling waves in glee:
A poet could not but be gay,
In such a jocund company:
I gazed—and gazed—but little thought
What wealth the show to me had brought:

For oft, when on my couch I lie
In vacant or in pensive mood,
They flash upon that inward eye
Which is the bliss of solitude;
And then my heart with pleasure fills,
And dances with the daffodils.

questions.model:
The final stanza changes the poem from a description of a beautiful scene into a reflection on the lasting power of memory and imagination. The first three stanzas are in the past tense and record what the speaker saw, but the last moves into a habitual present: "For oft, when on my couch I lie". The real value of the daffodils lies not in the moment itself but in its recollection.

The third stanza prepares for this turn. The speaker admits that he "gazed—and gazed—but little thought / What wealth the show to me had brought", the dashes slowing the line to suggest absorbed looking. The financial metaphor of "wealth" implies that the experience was stored and could be drawn on later.

The final stanza shows that wealth being spent. The daffodils "flash upon that inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude": the imagination becomes a kind of sight, and solitude, a source of loneliness in the first line, is redefined as "bliss". The closing line, in which the heart "dances with the daffodils", completes the change: the speaker now joins in the dance he once only watched, so the poem ends with a transformed self rather than a picture.

questions.model:
Taken as a whole, the poem suggests that nature does more than delight the individual: it enters the mind, heals isolation and becomes a permanent part of the self.

The relationship begins with separation. The speaker "wandered lonely as a cloud", a simile that places him within the landscape yet drifting above it, detached from human company. The daffodils immediately offer company: they are "a crowd, / A host", so the natural world answers human loneliness with community. The second stanza expands this into something vast. The flowers are "Continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the milky way", and the hyperbole "Ten thousand saw I at a glance" suggests an abundance that links a single lakeside to the whole cosmos. The individual is small, but he is included in an ordered, joyful universe.

The third stanza turns observation into participation in feeling: "A poet could not but be gay, / In such a jocund company". Joy here is almost involuntary, as though nature's mood simply passes into the human heart. Yet the poem insists that the deepest relationship is formed later, in memory. Through "that inward eye", the daffodils become part of the speaker's inner life and can return whenever he is "In vacant or in pensive mood".

Drawing these ideas together, the poem presents a Romantic belief that nature and the imagination work in partnership. The individual does not simply look at nature; he absorbs it, and by the last line, where his heart "dances with the daffodils", the boundary between self and landscape has dissolved. Nature becomes a lasting source of joy that transforms solitude itself.

sets.title: Futility
sets.author: Wilfred Owen
sets.source: Futility, in Poems (ed. Siegfried Sassoon), Chatto & Windus, 1920 (first published in The Nation, 1918)
sets.headnote: Wilfred Owen wrote this short lyric in 1918 while serving in the First World War; it was one of only five poems published in his lifetime. A soldier has died in the snow, and his comrades carry him into the sunlight.
sets.body:
Move him into the sun—
Gently its touch awoke him once,
At home, whispering of fields half-sown.
Always it woke him, even in France,
Until this morning and this snow.
If anything might rouse him now
The kind old sun will know.

Think how it wakes the seeds—
Woke once the clays of a cold star.
Are limbs, so dear-achieved, are sides
Full-nerved, still warm, too hard to stir?
Was it for this the clay grew tall?
—O what made fatuous sunbeams toil
To break earth's sleep at all?

The soldier's body becomes the result of that vast process: his limbs are "so dear-achieved", the product of ages of growth. This raises an unbearable question: "Was it for this the clay grew tall?" If life evolved only to be destroyed in war, then creation seems pointless. The final question calls the sunbeams "fatuous", meaning foolish, so the "kind old sun" of the first stanza is now mocked. One death has made the speaker doubt the purpose of all existence.

questions.model:
Owen shapes this two-stanza lyric so that its form traces the speaker's collapse from tender hope into anguished questioning.

The first stanza is built on gentle statements and an imperative. "Move him into the sun—" is a soft command, and "Gently" placed at the start of the next line slows the reading. The syntax is calm and narrative, recalling home and routine, and the line "Always it woke him, even in France," stresses habit and continuity. That continuity is broken by "Until this morning and this snow": the monosyllables and repeated "this" pin down the moment of death, and the cold "snow" opposes the warmth of the sun. The stanza closes in tentative faith, "The kind old sun will know", but the conditional "If anything" already admits doubt.

Sound reinforces the unease. Owen uses half-rhyme throughout, "once" with "France", "seeds" with "sides", "star" with "stir". The near-misses give the poem a muted, dissonant music, as though harmony itself had failed, which suits a world in which the sun cannot do its work.

In the second stanza the syntax shifts from statement to question. The speaker asks whether limbs "Full-nerved, still warm" are "too hard to stir", the caesuras and piled adjectives conveying desperate disbelief. Then the questions grow larger and more bitter: "Was it for this the clay grew tall?" The final question is broken off by a dash and a cry, "—O what made fatuous sunbeams toil / To break earth's sleep at all?", and the half-rhyme of "tall", "toil" and "all" chimes like a dying fall. The poem ends not with an answer but with despair, its form mirroring a faith that has been disturbed beyond repair.

sets.title: When I have fears that I may cease to be
sets.author: John Keats
sets.source: When I have fears that I may cease to be (written 1818), in Life, Letters, and Literary Remains of John Keats (ed. R. M. Milnes), 1848
sets.headnote: John Keats, an English Romantic poet, wrote this sonnet in January 1818, aged twenty-two. He had trained as a surgeon and had nursed his mother and brother through tuberculosis; he died of the disease himself in 1821.
sets.body:
When I have fears that I may cease to be
Before my pen has glean'd my teeming brain,
Before high-piled books, in charactery,
Hold like rich garners the full ripen'd grain;
When I behold, upon the night's starr'd face,
Huge cloudy symbols of a high romance,
And think that I may never live to trace
Their shadows, with the magic hand of chance;
And when I feel, fair creature of an hour,
That I shall never look upon thee more,
Never have relish in the faery power
Of unreflecting love;—then on the shore
Of the wide world I stand alone, and think
Till love and fame to nothingness do sink.

questions.model:
Keats structures this Shakespearean sonnet as a single long sentence in which fear accumulates clause by clause until it is released in the couplet. The anaphora of time clauses, "When I have fears", "When I behold" and "And when I feel", delays the main verb, so the reader is held in suspense just as the speaker is held in anxiety.

Each quatrain adds a new loss. The first fears the loss of poetic achievement, the "high-piled books" never written; the second the loss of imaginative vision, the "Huge cloudy symbols of a high romance" he may never "trace"; the third the loss of love, the "fair creature of an hour". The movement is from public ambition to private feeling, and the losses grow more personal.

The turn arrives late, in the middle of line 12: "—then on the shore / Of the wide world I stand alone". The dash marks the long-delayed main clause, and the enjambment pushes the reader across the line break to the edge of the "wide world", where the speaker appears as a solitary figure facing the sea. The couplet completes the sentence: he thinks "Till love and fame to nothingness do sink." The inverted syntax places "sink" at the very end, so the rhythm itself falls. The structure turns the poem's fears into a contemplative calm: by facing mortality, the speaker sees that love and fame matter less than he believed.

questions.model:
The poem presents the conflict between desire and mortality very effectively, because Keats makes desire so rich and sensuous that the threat of losing it becomes acute, and then ends with a resolution that is ambiguous rather than comforting.

Desire is expressed through imagery of fullness. His mind is a "teeming brain", his future books "rich garners" full of "ripen'd grain", and the night sky offers "Huge cloudy symbols of a high romance". Even love has "faery power", a magical, carefree force described as "unreflecting". Every desire is for abundance and intensity. Against this, mortality is announced in the stark opening phrase "cease to be", and transience appears in the beloved, a "fair creature of an hour". The contrast between infinite aspiration and limited time is the poem's central tension, and the repeated "Never" in lines 10 and 11 hammers home what death will take.

The ending is the poem's most powerful feature because it refuses easy consolation. Standing "on the shore / Of the wide world", the speaker confronts vastness alone, and love and fame "to nothingness do sink". This could be read as a hard-won calm, in which the perspective of mortality frees him from ambition, or as despair, in which everything he values dissolves. The ambiguity is honest, and it makes the conflict feel unresolved rather than neatly solved.

Knowing that Keats had watched his mother and brother die of tuberculosis, and would die at twenty-five, gives the poem great poignancy, but its effectiveness does not depend on biography. The precise imagery and controlled structure make the struggle between longing and limitation universal, which is why the poem succeeds.

sets.title: The Lake Isle of Innisfree
sets.author: W. B. Yeats
sets.source: The Lake Isle of Innisfree, in The Countess Kathleen and Various Legends and Lyrics, 1892 (first published 1890)
sets.headnote: W. B. Yeats was an Irish poet. He wrote this lyric in 1888 while living in London, after a shop-window fountain reminded him of the lakes of County Sligo, where he spent much of his childhood. Innisfree is a small island in Lough Gill.
sets.body:
I will arise and go now, and go to Innisfree,
And a small cabin build there, of clay and wattles made:
Nine bean-rows will I have there, a hive for the honey-bee,
And live alone in the bee-loud glade.

And I shall have some peace there, for peace comes dropping slow,
Dropping from the veils of the morning to where the cricket sings;
There midnight's all a glimmer, and noon a purple glow,
And evening full of the linnet's wings.

I will arise and go now, for always night and day
I hear lake water lapping with low sounds by the shore;
While I stand on the roadway, or on the pavements grey,
I hear it in the deep heart's core.

questions.model:
Yeats makes the peace of Innisfree audible. The poem's slow rhythms, repetitions and soft sounds enact the tranquillity the speaker longs for, so that the reader experiences the island's calm even as the speaker remains in the city.

The rhythm is unhurried from the start. The long lines, each with a pause near the middle, "I will arise and go now, and go to Innisfree", move like a measured chant, and the archaic, biblical cadence of "I will arise and go" gives the decision a solemn weight. Each stanza then closes with a shorter line, "And live alone in the bee-loud glade", which settles the stanza like an exhalation. The compound "bee-loud" is a striking piece of sound imagery: the island is not silent, but filled with a steady, natural hum.

The second stanza turns peace into a physical substance. "For peace comes dropping slow, / Dropping from the veils of the morning to where the cricket sings": the repetition of "dropping" across the line break slows the reading, so peace seems to fall gradually, like dew or mist. The phrase "the veils of the morning" adds softness, and the stanza moves through the day, from morning to "midnight's all a glimmer", "noon a purple glow" and "evening full of the linnet's wings", its gentle listing imitating the slow passing of time in a place without urgency.

The final stanza intensifies the music. "I hear lake water lapping with low sounds by the shore" is dense with alliteration of the letter l and long vowels, imitating the soft, regular movement of water against the bank. This sound persists "always night and day", and it reaches inward in the last line, "I hear it in the deep heart's core", where four heavy stresses slow the voice almost to a stop. By ending with sound rather than sight, Yeats suggests that peace is something felt inside, and the poem's music lets the reader share that inner experience.

sets.title: “Hope” is the thing with feathers
sets.author: Emily Dickinson
sets.source: “Hope” is the thing with feathers (c. 1861), first published in Poems, Second Series, 1891; text from the poet's manuscript version
sets.headnote: Emily Dickinson was an American poet who lived most of her life in her family home in Amherst, Massachusetts, and published almost nothing in her lifetime. The dashes and capital letters in this short lyric are her own.
sets.body:
“Hope” is the thing with feathers –
That perches in the soul –
And sings the tune without the words –
And never stops – at all –

And sweetest – in the Gale – is heard –
And sore must be the storm –
That could abash the little Bird
That kept so many warm –

I've heard it in the chillest land –
And on the strangest Sea –
Yet – never – in Extremity,
It asked a crumb – of Me.

Hope is "the thing with feathers" that "perches in the soul", suggesting it is light, fragile and always ready, resting within us rather than arriving from outside. It "sings the tune without the words", so hope comforts instinctively, beyond reason or explanation, and it "never stops – at all", implying constancy. The bird even shelters others, having "kept so many warm". The metaphor ends with hope's generosity: although the speaker has carried it through hardship, "It asked a crumb – of Me." Unlike a real bird that must be fed, hope sustains us without demanding anything in return.

questions.model:
Dickinson's punctuation and form make the reader slow down and feel the weight of individual words, so that a simple hymn-like poem becomes reflective and emphatic.

The dashes are her most distinctive device. In "And never stops – at all –", the dash creates a pause that isolates "at all", turning a casual phrase into a firm declaration of hope's constancy. In "Yet – never – in Extremity," the word "never" is framed on both sides, as though the speaker pauses to insist on it. The dashes also mimic the halting movement of thought, as if the speaker is weighing her words, and they leave many lines open-ended, suggesting the song continues beyond them.

The form is equally purposeful. The short quatrains and alternating line lengths echo the common metre of church hymns, giving the poem a familiar, consoling music appropriate to a subject like hope. Yet Dickinson unsettles the pattern with slant rhyme, as in "storm" and "warm" or "Sea" and "Me", so the poem sounds harmonious but not quite resolved, mirroring hope in a world of hardship.

Capitalisation adds emphasis: "Gale", "Sea" and "Extremity" are given the status of forces, while the final capitalised "Me" places the speaker herself in the closing position. The effect is a voice that seems simple but makes the reader linger on every turn of thought.

questions.model:
The view is largely convincing, but it needs refining. Dickinson presents hope as remarkably enduring, more persistent than any hardship the speaker has known, yet she also acknowledges that hope is small and that a severe enough storm could disturb it. Its strength lies not in power but in persistence.

The poem's central claim is hope's constancy. It "never stops – at all", and the dash and final placement of "at all" make this sound absolute. Hope is most audible precisely in adversity: "And sweetest – in the Gale – is heard". The paradox is important: the song is sweetest when conditions are worst, so hardship does not diminish hope but reveals its value.

However, Dickinson does not make hope invincible. The bird is "little", a creature of feathers, and the lines "And sore must be the storm – / That could abash the little Bird" concede that some storm could, at least in principle, unsettle it. The verb "abash" means to disconcert or shame, not to destroy, which suggests that even at worst hope is silenced only momentarily. The point is not that hope is stronger than hardship in force, but that it would take an extraordinary hardship to overcome it, and that hope has "kept so many warm" through ordinary ones.

The final stanza grounds the claim in personal testimony. "I've heard it in the chillest land – / And on the strangest Sea –": the superlatives suggest the most extreme isolation and uncertainty, and the speaker has found hope present in both. The closing lines then add a different kind of strength: "Yet – never – in Extremity, / It asked a crumb – of Me." Hope is not only resilient but entirely unselfish, demanding nothing even when the speaker has nothing to give.

Overall, Dickinson suggests that hope is a comfort that outlasts hardship rather than one that defeats it. By admitting its smallness and vulnerability, she makes its persistence more moving, so the poem's vision of hope is both realistic and deeply consoling.

sets.title: When You Are Old
sets.author: W. B. Yeats
sets.source: When You Are Old, in The Countess Kathleen and Various Legends and Lyrics, 1892
sets.headnote: W. B. Yeats wrote this lyric in 1891, loosely adapting a sonnet by the French Renaissance poet Pierre de Ronsard. It is usually read as addressed to Maud Gonne, the Irish revolutionary whom Yeats loved for many years and who repeatedly refused his proposals of marriage.
sets.body:
When you are old and grey and full of sleep,
And nodding by the fire, take down this book,
And slowly read, and dream of the soft look
Your eyes had once, and of their shadows deep;

How many loved your moments of glad grace,
And loved your beauty with love false or true,
But one man loved the pilgrim soul in you,
And loved the sorrows of your changing face;

And bending down beside the glowing bars,
Murmur, a little sadly, how Love fled
And paced upon the mountains overhead
And hid his face amid a crowd of stars.

questions.model: The second stanza contrasts the "many" who were attracted to the woman's surface with the "one man" who loved her inner self. Others loved her "moments of glad grace" and "your beauty with love false or true", a love tied to youth and appearance and possibly insincere. The turn on "But" sets the speaker apart: he "loved the pilgrim soul in you", her searching, restless spirit, and "the sorrows of your changing face". The repetition of "loved" four times makes the stanza a catalogue of devotions, culminating in his, which embraces her sadness and ageing. His love is presented as deeper and more lasting because it does not depend on beauty that time will take.

questions.model:
Yeats creates a tone of tender regret by imagining the beloved in old age, so that the speaker's present unreturned love is recast as a quiet prophecy of what she will one day understand.

The opening image is gentle and domestic: "When you are old and grey and full of sleep, / And nodding by the fire". The polysyndeton of "and" slows the line, mimicking the drowsy pace of age, and the fireside setting suggests comfort rather than decay. There is no bitterness here; the speaker imagines her old age with care.

The instruction to "take down this book" is self-reflexive: the book is the poem itself. The speaker imagines his words outlasting their love affair and returning her to memories of "the soft look / Your eyes had once". The poem becomes a vessel of memory, and its quiet authority suggests he knows its value will be recognised too late.

The final stanza intensifies the regret. Bending "beside the glowing bars" of the fire, she will "Murmur, a little sadly", a careful understatement that implies sorrow without despair. Love itself is then personified: he "fled / And paced upon the mountains overhead / And hid his face amid a crowd of stars". The imagery lifts from the hearth to the sky, making lost love vast, remote and almost divine. Love is not destroyed but withdrawn beyond reach. The combination of the intimate fireside and the distant stars captures the poem's tone exactly: a tender, wistful recognition of something precious that was offered and not taken.

questions.model:
The speaker's attitude is best seen as devoted but not wholly selfless: his love is genuine, yet the poem is also a gentle act of persuasion that asks to be remembered.

The evidence for selflessness is strong. He loves "the pilgrim soul in you" and "the sorrows of your changing face", qualities that do not flatter him and that will outlast her youth. He imagines her old age tenderly, "nodding by the fire", without any wish for her suffering.

Yet the poem's structure suggests self-interest. It is a series of instructions, "take down this book, / And slowly read, and dream", imagining her reading his own words and recognising his worth. The comparison with the many who loved her "with love false or true" implies that he alone was sincere, and the final image of her murmuring "a little sadly" imagines her regret at refusing him.

The most convincing reading is that both attitudes coexist. His love is real, but he wants it to be understood, even if only when it is too late; the tenderness of the tone softens what is, at heart, a plea.

sets.title: Dover Beach
sets.author: Matthew Arnold
sets.source: Dover Beach, in New Poems, Macmillan, 1867 (probably written c. 1851)
sets.headnote: Matthew Arnold was an English poet and critic. The poem is set at night at Dover, on the English Channel, and is spoken to a companion, probably his wife. It was written as scientific discoveries were unsettling traditional religious belief in Victorian England.
sets.body:
The sea is calm to-night.
The tide is full, the moon lies fair
Upon the straits;—on the French coast the light
Gleams and is gone; the cliffs of England stand,
Glimmering and vast, out in the tranquil bay.
Come to the window, sweet is the night-air!
Only, from the long line of spray
Where the sea meets the moon-blanch'd land,
Listen! you hear the grating roar
Of pebbles which the waves draw back, and fling,
At their return, up the high strand,
Begin, and cease, and then again begin,
With tremulous cadence slow, and bring
The eternal note of sadness in.

Sophocles long ago
Heard it on the Ægæan, and it brought
Into his mind the turbid ebb and flow
Of human misery; we
Find also in the sound a thought,
Hearing it by this distant northern sea.

The Sea of Faith
Was once, too, at the full, and round earth's shore
Lay like the folds of a bright girdle furl'd.
But now I only hear
Its melancholy, long, withdrawing roar,
Retreating, to the breath
Of the night-wind, down the vast edges drear
And naked shingles of the world.

Ah, love, let us be true
To one another! for the world, which seems
To lie before us like a land of dreams,
So various, so beautiful, so new,
Hath really neither joy, nor love, nor light,
Nor certitude, nor peace, nor help for pain;
And we are here as on a darkling plain
Swept with confused alarms of struggle and flight,
Where ignorant armies clash by night.

questions.model: The first stanza begins in serene beauty but ends in sadness. The opening is calm and visual: "The sea is calm to-night. / The tide is full, the moon lies fair", and the cliffs stand "Glimmering and vast, out in the tranquil bay". The speaker even invites his companion to share the moment: "sweet is the night-air!" The word "Only" marks a turn from sight to sound. He asks her to "Listen!" to "the grating roar / Of pebbles", and the harsh adjective "grating" disturbs the peace. The repeated rhythm "Begin, and cease, and then again begin" imitates the endless motion of the waves, which bring "The eternal note of sadness in". Beneath the calm surface, the speaker hears a permanent melancholy.

questions.model:
Arnold transforms the literal sea at Dover into an extended metaphor for religious faith, and the ebbing tide becomes an image of belief withdrawing from the modern world, leaving it exposed and comfortless.

The metaphor is prepared in the first stanza, where the speaker hears in the waves "The eternal note of sadness". The second stanza widens this to human history: Sophocles heard the same sound and thought of "the turbid ebb and flow / Of human misery". The tide's movement becomes a pattern of human suffering, so the sea is already a symbol before Arnold names it.

The third stanza makes the metaphor explicit: "The Sea of Faith / Was once, too, at the full". In the past, faith encircled the world "like the folds of a bright girdle furl'd", a simile of protection, unity and brightness, as though belief held the world together like a belt or sash. The past tense "Was once" immediately signals that this time is over.

The present is captured through sound: "But now I only hear / Its melancholy, long, withdrawing roar". The listing of adjectives and the long vowel sounds stretch the line out, enacting the slow retreat of the tide and the speaker's prolonged grief. The enjambment of "Retreating, to the breath / Of the night-wind" carries the sound away into darkness. What remains is "the vast edges drear / And naked shingles of the world", an image of bare pebbled beach that suggests a world stripped of meaning and protection. The inverted "edges drear" and the word "naked" make the loss feel cold and vulnerable.

In its Victorian context, when geology and evolutionary science were challenging literal readings of scripture, the metaphor captures a whole culture's crisis. Arnold does not argue against faith; he mourns its retreat. By grounding a spiritual loss in the physical sound and sight of an ebbing sea, he makes doubt something the reader can hear and feel.

questions.model:
The poem suggests that, once religious faith has retreated, the only thing individuals can hold on to is faithfulness to one another, though even this refuge is fragile.

The final stanza turns from the sea to the companion: "Ah, love, let us be true / To one another!" The exclamation makes loyalty an urgent necessity rather than a romantic gesture. Fidelity between two people replaces the lost "Sea of Faith".

This is necessary because the world is deceptive. It "seems / To lie before us like a land of dreams, / So various, so beautiful, so new", but "Hath really neither joy, nor love, nor light". The long negative list strips away every consolation, including certainty and "help for pain".

The closing image shows how small the refuge is. The lovers stand "as on a darkling plain" where "ignorant armies clash by night", a vision of confusion and violence without purpose. Drawing these ideas together, the poem offers human love as the one remaining light, but a light kept alive in darkness and threat.

sets.title: I Will Fight No More Forever
sets.author: Chief Joseph (Nez Perce)
sets.source: Surrender speech, Bear Paw, Montana Territory, 5 October 1877, as recorded in English by Lt Charles Erskine Scott Wood; printed in Harper's Weekly, 17 November 1877
sets.headnote: Chief Joseph was a leader of the Nez Perce people of the American Northwest. In 1877, after a retreat of more than 1,500 miles from the US Army, the Nez Perce were surrounded near the Canadian border. This is the English version of his surrender message to General Oliver Howard, delivered through an interpreter; historians debate how closely the recorded words match what he said.
sets.body: Tell General Howard I know his heart. What he told me before, I have it in my heart. I am tired of fighting. Our chiefs are killed. Looking Glass is dead. Too-hul-hul-sote is dead. The old men are all dead. It is the young men who say yes or no. He who led on the young men is dead. It is cold, and we have no blankets. The little children are freezing to death. My people, some of them, have run away to the hills, and have no blankets, no food; no one knows where they are—perhaps freezing to death. I want to have time to look for my children and see how many of them I can find. Maybe I shall find them among the dead. Hear me, my chiefs. I am tired; my heart is sick and sad. From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever.

questions.model:
The speech conveys defeat and dignity with remarkable effectiveness, because Joseph admits total loss without ever surrendering his authority or self-respect.

Defeat is stated with unflinching honesty. "I am tired of fighting" opens his admission, and the speech closes its personal statement with "I am tired; my heart is sick and sad." The roll call of the dead and the image of children "freezing to death" make clear that the Nez Perce cannot continue. There is no attempt to disguise the loss.

Yet the speech is framed with dignity. It opens not with pleading but with a message between equals: "Tell General Howard I know his heart." Joseph speaks as one leader to another, trusting Howard's earlier word. His concern is not for himself but for his people: "I want to have time to look for my children and see how many of them I can find." The imperative "Hear me, my chiefs" shows that he still speaks as a leader, explaining his decision to those he is responsible for.

The final sentence fuses the two qualities most powerfully. "From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever" marks the moment of surrender with an image from the natural world, giving it the solemnity of an oath. The absolute "no more forever" accepts defeat completely, but the choice is presented as his own decision, made freely and with composure.

It is worth remembering that the words reached their audience through an interpreter and a recorder, so their polish may owe something to translation. Even so, the plain, measured voice that survives makes defeat feel noble rather than humiliating, which is why the speech remains so moving.

sets.title: Letter to Mrs Bixby
sets.author: Abraham Lincoln
sets.source: Letter to Mrs Lydia Bixby, 21 November 1864, printed in the Boston Evening Transcript, 25 November 1864
sets.headnote: During the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln sent this letter of condolence to a Boston widow believed to have lost five sons fighting for the Union. Later research showed that two of the sons had died; some historians think Lincoln's secretary John Hay drafted the letter.
sets.body:
Dear Madam,—I have been shown in the files of the War Department a statement of the Adjutant General of Massachusetts that you are the mother of five sons who have died gloriously on the field of battle. I feel how weak and fruitless must be any word of mine which should attempt to beguile you from the grief of a loss so overwhelming. But I cannot refrain from tendering you the consolation that may be found in the thanks of the Republic they died to save. I pray that our Heavenly Father may assuage the anguish of your bereavement, and leave you only the cherished memory of the loved and lost, and the solemn pride that must be yours to have laid so costly a sacrifice upon the altar of freedom.

Yours, very sincerely and respectfully,
A. Lincoln.

questions.model:
The letter begins its consolation by admitting that consolation is almost impossible. The writer says he feels "how weak and fruitless must be any word of mine which should attempt to beguile you from the grief of a loss so overwhelming." The adjectives "weak and fruitless" are humble, and the verb "beguile" suggests that words could only distract her rather than heal her. By recognising the scale of her loss first, he avoids seeming glib.

The turn comes with "But I cannot refrain from tendering you the consolation". "Cannot refrain" suggests an obligation he feels personally, and "tendering" is a formal, respectful word, as though offering a gift. Crucially, the comfort is not his own: it lies in "the thanks of the Republic they died to save" and in a prayer that "our Heavenly Father may assuage the anguish". By placing consolation in the nation and in God, rather than in his own eloquence, the writer remains consistent with his opening humility while still giving the mother something to hold.

questions.model:
The view is persuasive. The letter genuinely honours the mother's grief, but it also frames that grief in a way that supports the Union's war effort, and the two purposes are woven together so closely that they are hard to separate.

The letter's respect for private grief is clear. It acknowledges "a loss so overwhelming" and admits that any words must be "weak and fruitless". It prays that God will "assuage the anguish of your bereavement", naming her pain directly rather than dismissing it. The hope that she will keep "the cherished memory of the loved and lost" is tender, recognising her sons as individuals she loved, not simply soldiers.

Yet the letter also turns these deaths into national meaning. The sons "died gloriously on the field of battle", an adverb that presents war death as honourable, and the consolation offered is "the thanks of the Republic they died to save". This reframes private loss as a contribution to a cause, implicitly justifying the war's cost. The final metaphor is the clearest example: she is to feel "the solemn pride that must be yours to have laid so costly a sacrifice upon the altar of freedom." The religious image of an altar makes her sons' deaths a sacred offering, and the modal "must be yours" gently tells her what to feel. Grief is to be accompanied, even transformed, by pride.

Context strengthens this reading. The letter was printed in a Boston newspaper within days, so it reached a public audience at a time when the Union needed continued support for the war. Its emphasis on glory and freedom would have spoken to every grieving family. The later discovery that not all five sons had died for the Union adds an irony, suggesting that the letter's symbolic purpose mattered as much as its factual basis.

Overall, the letter does both things at once. Its humility and compassion are real, but its consolation is inseparable from a national story of sacrifice, which is precisely what makes it such a powerful public document.

sets.title: Sonnet 18 (Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?)
sets.author: William Shakespeare
sets.source: Sonnet 18, in Shake-speares Sonnets, Thomas Thorpe, 1609 (spelling modernised as in standard editions)
sets.headnote: William Shakespeare's 154 sonnets were published in 1609. Sonnet 18 belongs to a group addressed to a young man whom the speaker admires; in Elizabethan English a 'lease' is a fixed-term rental and 'thou ow'st' means 'you own'.
sets.body:
Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer's lease hath all too short a date;
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm'd;
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance or nature's changing course untrimm'd;
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow'st;
Nor shall Death brag thou wander'st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou grow'st:
So long as men can breathe or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

questions.model: The speaker raises a conventional comparison only to reject it. His answer to the opening question is that the beloved is "more lovely and more temperate", meaning more beautiful and more even in nature. Summer, by contrast, is flawed. It is unstable, since "Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May", and it is brief: "summer's lease hath all too short a date", a legal metaphor suggesting that summer is only rented for a limited term. Even the sun is unreliable, "Sometime too hot" and often "dimm'd" by cloud. By cataloguing summer's imperfections, the speaker turns a familiar compliment into a stronger one: the beloved surpasses the best that nature can offer.

questions.model:
The first eight lines dwell on decline: summer fades and "every fair from fair sometime declines". At line 9 the volta reverses this movement: "But thy eternal summer shall not fade". The beloved's beauty becomes a summer that does not end, an oxymoron that defies the natural cycle just described.

The third quatrain extends this defiance to death itself. "Nor shall Death brag thou wander'st in his shade" personifies Death as a boastful figure who will be denied his triumph, and the repeated negatives, "shall not", "Nor lose", "Nor shall", build a sense of certainty. The reason is given in the next line: the beloved will live "When in eternal lines to time thou grow'st". "Lines" puns on lines of poetry and on lineage, but the couplet makes the primary meaning clear.

The final couplet is balanced and emphatic: "So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee." The parallel "So long" clauses stretch the claim across all of human time, and the repeated "this" points to the sonnet itself. The poem shifts from praising the beloved to praising its own power: poetry, not nature, is what grants immortality.

questions.model:
The sonnet suggests that time inevitably destroys natural beauty, but that art can rescue beauty from time by fixing it in words that outlast the body.

In the first eight lines, time governs everything beautiful. Summer exists on a "lease" with "all too short a date", and the sun's "gold complexion" is "dimm'd". The general law is stated plainly: "every fair from fair sometime declines, / By chance or nature's changing course untrimm'd". Whether by accident or by the ordinary processes of nature, beauty is stripped away. Beauty here is not a lasting possession but something on loan.

Art enters as the answer to this law. The beloved's "eternal summer shall not fade" because they will live "in eternal lines", growing alongside time rather than being consumed by it. The verb "grow'st" is striking: in poetry the beloved does not decline but increases, reversing nature's pattern. The final couplet makes the claim universal: "So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee." Art's life depends only on readers, and while there are readers it confers life.

Drawing these ideas together, the poem presents beauty as the subject, time as the enemy and art as the victor. Yet there is an irony. The beloved is never named or physically described, so what survives is not the person but the poem's praise. The sonnet's confidence is therefore partly a claim for poetry itself: Shakespeare's verse has indeed outlived its subject, which suggests that art's real triumph over time is its own survival, carrying beauty as an idea rather than as a living face.
